column4: Last lesson you learned to build an options trade on a thesis instead of a wish, and to respect the clock working against a buyer. Today we zoom out to the rule underneath every trade you will ever place. Here's the first job of an investor, and it's not the one most people think. Before you chase a single gain, your real job is to not get wiped out. Protect the money first. In the next few minutes you'll learn how to size a trade so no single loss can hurt you, where to place a stop, and how to judge whether a setup is even worth the risk. Get this part right and you get to stay in the game long enough for everything else to work.

Rule one is simple: risk management means protecting your capital. Here's why it matters so much. You cannot compound from zero. Lose it all on one bad bet and there's nothing left to grow, no matter how good your next idea is. That leads straight to the risk-return tradeoff on screen. Higher potential reward almost always comes with higher risk, and the two move together. So when someone promises high returns with no risk, treat that as the loudest warning sign there is. Protecting the downside is what keeps you alive to catch the upside.

Now the rule that puts protection into a number: risk no more than one to two percent of your account on any single trade. Look at the thin red slice on the pie. That's all one trade is allowed to cost you. Why so small? Because even a brutal losing streak can't ruin you when each loss is tiny. Ten losses in a row at one percent each still leaves most of your account intact. There are a few ways to size a position: a fixed dollar amount, a fixed percent of the portfolio, or risk-based sizing that works backward from the loss you're willing to take. That last one is the pro's method, and it's what we'll use in the calculator.

Two tools turn that rule into action. First, the stop-loss. It's an order that sells at a preset price to cap your loss, the safety net that catches a falling trade before it wrecks the account. Second, reward-to-risk, or R to R. Watch the diagram: your entry sits in the middle, your stop below it, your target above. R to R simply compares the distance up to your target against the distance down to your stop. Favor setups where the reward clearly outweighs the risk, something like two to one, so your winners more than pay for your losers. These numbers are illustrative, just the shape of the idea.

Your turn to run the math the way a professional does. Set your account size, drag the risk percent, then enter a price and a stop. The calculator works backward: it figures the risk per share from the gap between entry and stop, caps your total dollars at risk to your chosen percent, and tells you exactly how many shares that allows. Change the stop and watch the share count move. A tighter stop lets you hold more shares for the same risk; a wider stop means fewer. Every number here is illustrative, a tool for practice, not advice.

Let's make the habits stick. Sort these behaviors yourself. Tap a card to pick it up, then drop it in the column where it belongs. One column protects your capital, the disciplined moves that keep you in the game. The other blows up the account, the reckless ones that end it. As you sort, notice the pattern: protection is always about capping the downside before you ever think about the upside.
Five quick questions to lock it in. Answer them to earn your points for the lesson.

Carry these four with you. Protect the capital first, because you can't compound from zero. Risk only one to two percent on any single trade. Set a stop before you enter, so every loss is capped. And take setups where the reward clearly outweighs the risk. You've got the math of survival. But the hardest part isn't the math, it's you. Next up, in lesson five point two, we tackle trading psychology and the trade journal, the discipline that actually makes you follow these rules when real money is on the line.
